title: Proving It to the World
summary: After their first flights, the Wright brothers practised in a cow field until they could fly in big circles for more than half an hour. But they kept their airplane hidden, and many people called them liars, until Wilbur flew in France in 1908 and amazed everyone who watched.

sections.heading: Flying in a Cow Pasture
paragraphs: The 1903 Flyer had made history, but it had also been wrecked by a gust of wind, and it had only ever flown in straight lines for less than a minute. A machine like that was not much use to anyone. Wilbur and Orville Wright knew they still had a lot to learn. They needed a practice field closer to home, where they could fly week after week without travelling hundreds of kilometres to the sand dunes of North Carolina.

They found it about 13 kilometres (8 miles) northeast of Dayton, Ohio. It was a big, bumpy pasture called Huffman Prairie, owned by a Dayton banker named Torrence Huffman. He let the brothers use it without paying any rent. The only condition was that they had to move his cows and horses out of the way before they flew. The field was not perfect. It was dotted with tree stumps and anthills, a tall thorny tree stood near one edge, and the winds were weaker and more changeable than at Kitty Hawk. But it had one great advantage: an electric trolley line ran past it, so the brothers could ride out from their bicycle shop in Dayton whenever the weather looked good.

Their new machine, the Flyer II, looked a lot like the 1903 Flyer, but it had a new, slightly more powerful engine and sturdier parts. In May 1904 the brothers invited newspaper reporters out to see it fly. It was a flop. The engine was not running well and the wind died away, and the machine just slid off the end of its launching rail. A second try a few days later ended with a short hop and a heavy landing. The reporters went home unimpressed, and most newspapers decided the story of the flying brothers was not worth following.

Without strong winds to help, the Flyer II struggled to get up to flying speed on its short wooden launching rail. So in September 1904 the Wrights built a clever starting device. It was a tall wooden tower, called a derrick, with a heavy weight hanging from the top. A rope ran from the weight, down through pulleys, and along the rail to the airplane. When the weight was released and fell, it yanked the airplane forward along the rail like a giant catapult. At first they used a weight of about 360 kilograms (800 pounds), and later they increased it to around 730 kilograms (1,600 pounds). With the catapult, they could take off even on calm days.

Now they could practise in earnest. The hardest thing to learn was turning. Going straight is one thing; banking a flying machine into a smooth, safe turn without sliding sideways or stalling is quite another. On 20 September 1904, Wilbur did something no one had ever done before. He flew the Flyer II all the way around in a complete circle, covering about 1,240 metres (4,080 feet) in 1 minute and 16 seconds, and landed safely back near where he had started.

One person outside the family saw it. His name was Amos Root, a businessman from Medina, Ohio, who published a magazine about beekeeping called Gleanings in Bee Culture. Root was fascinated by new technology, and he had travelled from his home to watch the brothers practise. He wrote an excited account of the circling flight for his beekeeping readers, describing it as like a locomotive without wheels, flying through the air on white wings. It was one of the first eyewitness reports of a powered airplane turning in the air, and it appeared not in a famous newspaper but in a magazine about bees.

By the end of 1904, the brothers had made 105 flights at Huffman Prairie. That sounds impressive, but most were very short, and all of them added together came to only about 49 minutes in the air. Their longest flight lasted just over 5 minutes. They had also crashed several times, because the Flyer II kept bobbing up and down in pitch. They even bolted about 32 kilograms of iron bars near the front elevator to try to calm it. Clearly, something about the design was still not right.

sections.heading: Flyer III: The First Truly Practical Airplane
paragraphs: Over the winter of 1904 to 1905, the Wrights built a third machine, the Flyer III. They reused the engine and much of the hardware from the Flyer II, and at first the new airplane looked and behaved much like the old one. On 14 July 1905, Orville crashed it badly. The Flyer swooped up and down, then slammed into the ground. The machine was badly smashed, but luckily Orville was only shaken and bruised.

Instead of patching it up, the brothers thought carefully about the problem. They rebuilt the Flyer III with a much bigger front elevator and a bigger rudder, and they moved both of them farther away from the wings. This gave the controls more leverage, the way a longer spanner makes it easier to turn a stubborn bolt. They also gave the pilot a separate control for the rudder, instead of linking it automatically to the wing warping. Now the pilot could combine roll and yaw however he needed. These changes fixed the bobbing problem that had troubled all their earlier machines.

The difference was dramatic. Within weeks, flights were lasting longer than 20 minutes. The brothers could bank, turn, fly figure-eights and circle the field again and again until their fuel ran out. They had learned to handle a powered airplane as surely as they had once learned to handle a bicycle.

On 5 October 1905, Wilbur took off and circled Huffman Prairie again and again. He stayed up for 39 minutes and 23 seconds and flew about 39 kilometres (24 miles). He only came down because the fuel tank was empty. That single flight was longer than all of their flights in 1903 and 1904 added together. Across 1905, the brothers made 50 flights and spent about 262 minutes, more than four hours, in the air.

Many historians call the 1905 Flyer III the world's first practical airplane: a machine that could take off, stay up for a long time, go where its pilot wanted, and land safely, again and again. The brothers knew exactly what they had achieved. And then, at the very moment they had solved the problem of flight, they stopped flying.

The Flyer III still exists. Today it is displayed in the Wright Brothers Aviation Center at Carillon Historical Park in Dayton, after a restoration that Orville himself helped with before his death in 1948. It is the only fixed-wing airplane that has been named a National Historic Landmark. Huffman Prairie is now part of Dayton Aviation Heritage National Historical Park, and it still looks much as it did then: a wide, grassy field.

sections.heading: Grounded on Purpose: Fliers or Liars?
paragraphs: Why would two inventors stop flying just when they had finally cracked it? The answer has to do with money, patents and fear of being copied.

The Wrights had spent years of their lives and much of their savings on flying. They believed their control system, the combination of wing warping, elevator and rudder that let a pilot balance and steer, was their great invention, and they wanted to be paid for it. In March 1903, even before their first powered flight, they had applied for a patent on their 1902 glider's control system. A patent is a legal document that gives an inventor the right to stop others from copying an invention without permission for a number of years. Their patent was finally granted on 22 May 1906, as US Patent number 821,393.

The brothers worried that if they flew in public, or let anyone photograph their airplane closely, clever rivals would copy their ideas before the patent was secure or before they had signed any deals. So they dismantled the Flyer III in November 1905 and did not fly at all in 1906 or 1907. Instead, they tried to sell their airplane to governments. In October 1905 they wrote to the United States War Department, the British War Office and others. But there was a catch: the Wrights refused to show the machine until a buyer signed a contract, and the buyers refused to sign a contract until they had seen it fly. The US Army's answer was that it would do nothing until a machine had actually been shown to fly with a pilot aboard.

Meanwhile, in Europe, especially in France, many aviation enthusiasts simply did not believe the Wrights' story. Two bicycle makers from Ohio, flying in circles for over half an hour, with hardly any photographs and no public demonstrations? It seemed too good to be true. French newspapers called the brothers 'bluffeurs', which means bluffers. In February 1906 the Paris edition of the New York Herald wrote that the Wrights were 'either fliers or liars'. Ernest Archdeacon, a leading member of the Aéro-Club de France, was openly scornful.

To be fair to the doubters, the Wrights had not given them much to go on. There were letters, a few reports from local people and Amos Root's article in a bee magazine. But science runs on evidence that others can check, and the brothers were keeping most of their evidence locked away. Their secrecy protected their invention, but it also meant that, for a few years, other inventors in Europe believed they were racing to be first, and the Wrights' reputation suffered.

sections.heading: Santos-Dumont and the 14-bis
paragraphs: While the Wrights' airplane sat in pieces in Dayton, Paris was buzzing with excitement about a small, stylish man from Brazil. Alberto Santos-Dumont was the son of a rich coffee-plantation owner, and he had moved to Paris as a young man. He was already famous there for flying airships, which are balloons shaped like long cigars with engines and propellers. Parisians had seen him float over the rooftops in his little airships, and the story goes that he sometimes parked one outside a café while he stopped for a drink.

In 1906 he turned to airplanes. His machine looked very strange to modern eyes. It was a biplane built from box-kite-like cells, inspired by Lawrence Hargrave's box kites from Part 4. The wings were at the back, and a box-shaped steering cell stuck out at the front, so the 14-bis seemed to fly tail-first. This front-steering layout is called a canard, from the French word for duck, because the long neck at the front reminded people of a duck in flight. The pilot stood up in a small basket. A light French Antoinette engine of about 50 horsepower drove a propeller at the back.

The odd name came from how it was first tested. Santos-Dumont hung the new airplane underneath his airship Number 14 to see how it behaved in the air, so he called it '14-bis', meaning something like '14 again' or '14 part two'.

On 13 September 1906 he managed a tiny hop of a few metres. On 23 October 1906, at the Bagatelle park on the edge of Paris, he flew more than 50 metres in front of official observers from the Aéro-Club de France, winning a prize for the first flight of over 25 metres. A delighted crowd cheered. Then he added control surfaces to the wings, an early form of the hinged flaps you will learn about in Part 12, to help keep the wings level. On 12 November 1906, again at Bagatelle, he flew about 220 metres in roughly 21 to 22 seconds, at a height of a few metres.

These were the first powered airplane flights in Europe to be officially watched and measured. For many people in France, and especially in Brazil, Santos-Dumont became the true hero of flight. He had flown in public, on wheels, from a standing start, without a catapult, and he was generous with his ideas: he did not try to keep his designs secret.

But compare the numbers. Santos-Dumont's best flight in 1906 lasted about 21 seconds and travelled in a nearly straight line. A year earlier, in their cow pasture in Ohio, the Wrights had flown in circles for 39 minutes. Most historians give Santos-Dumont fair credit as a brilliant, brave pioneer and Europe's first airplane flier, while recognising that the Wrights were far ahead in the hardest part of the problem: control.

sections.heading: Other Claims: Whitehead and Pearse
paragraphs: Whenever something important is invented, other people come forward, sometimes many years later, with stories that someone else did it first. Flying is no different. Two of the most famous rival claims come from opposite sides of the world.

Gustave Whitehead was a German-born mechanic living in Bridgeport, Connecticut. On 18 August 1901, a local newspaper, the Bridgeport Herald, printed an exciting article saying that four days earlier, Whitehead had flown his machine, called Number 21, about half a mile (800 metres) near Fairfield, Connecticut. The article had no author's name and was illustrated with a drawing, not a photograph. A photograph of the flight was supposedly taken, but no such picture has ever been found, and many researchers believe it never existed.

Since then, people have argued about Whitehead for more than a hundred years. In 2013, an editorial in the respected aircraft reference book Jane's All the World's Aircraft supported his claim, which caused a big stir, though the publisher later said the piece was the editor's personal opinion. That same year, the state of Connecticut passed a law honouring Whitehead's flight. But most aviation historians, including the Royal Aeronautical Society in Britain, have looked carefully at the evidence and concluded that it does not show a controlled, powered flight. Whitehead built engines and machines and clearly loved flying, but he left no reliable record, no surviving photograph of a flight, and no successful aircraft that others could copy.

Richard Pearse was a farmer and inventor near Waitohi, close to Temuka in the South Canterbury region of New Zealand. Working alone on his farm, he built a monoplane, an airplane with a single wing, made of bamboo and fabric, with an engine of his own design. Some people who lived nearby later remembered seeing him take off and land, possibly as early as 31 March 1903. In one account, his machine rose into the air and ended up stuck in a tall gorse hedge.

The trouble is that most of these memories were collected 50 years or more after the events, and the exact dates are uncertain. Pearse himself never claimed to have beaten the Wrights. In letters and interviews he described his early efforts as short, uncontrolled hops, and he suggested his serious attempts came after 1903. He was a remarkable, imaginative inventor working far from anyone who could help him, and New Zealand rightly remembers him. But there is no solid evidence that he made a sustained, controlled, powered flight.

This is a good lesson in how history works. Exciting stories are not enough. Historians need evidence: photographs, measurements, letters written at the time, independent witnesses, and machines that could be studied or copied. The Wrights, despite their secrecy, eventually had all of these.

sections.heading: Curtiss and the June Bug
paragraphs: Back in the United States, another team was getting into the air. In 1907, Alexander Graham Bell, the inventor of the telephone, formed a group called the Aerial Experiment Association. Bell was then about 60 years old and had been experimenting with giant kites at his summer home in Nova Scotia, Canada. His wife, Mabel Bell, helped pay for the association. Its young members included two Canadian engineers, Frederick 'Casey' Baldwin and John McCurdy; a US Army lieutenant named Thomas Selfridge, who would soon play a tragic part in this story; and an engine builder and motorcycle racer from Hammondsport, New York, named Glenn Curtiss, who held the title of fastest man on Earth after riding a V8 motorcycle at about 219 kilometres per hour in 1907.

Each member designed an airplane in turn. Selfridge designed the Red Wing, and later became the first US military officer to fly an airplane on his own, in the association's White Wing. The third machine was Curtiss's design, a biplane called the June Bug.

The magazine Scientific American had offered a trophy for the first public flight of over 1 kilometre in the United States. On 4 July 1908, at Hammondsport, in front of a crowd and official judges from the Aero Club of America, Curtiss flew the June Bug about 1,550 metres (5,085 feet) in 1 minute and 42 seconds and won the trophy. It was the first pre-announced public airplane flight in America, and it made Curtiss famous.

The June Bug did not use wing warping. Instead, it had small triangular movable surfaces at its wingtips that could be tilted to roll the airplane. But to the Wrights, that did not matter. Their patent, they believed, covered any system that changed the angle of the wings on the two sides to keep the airplane balanced, however it was done. Soon after the July flight, Orville wrote to Curtiss warning that the brothers had not given permission to use their system for exhibitions or to make money. Curtiss refused to pay for a licence.

This was the beginning of a long and bitter legal fight between the Wrights and Curtiss. In 1913 a court ruled in the Wrights' favour, but appeals and arguments dragged on for years. Some historians believe the patent battle slowed down American aviation, while Europe raced ahead. Others point out that the Wrights had a real right to protect an invention that had cost them years of work. It is still a lively debate.

sections.heading: August 1908: Wilbur Astonishes France
paragraphs: By 1908, the Wrights' long wait was finally paying off. On 8 February 1908, the US Army Signal Corps agreed to buy a Wright airplane, provided it passed a series of tough tests. Soon afterwards, the brothers also struck a deal with a group of French businessmen. Both deals required public flights. The brothers split up: Wilbur would fly in France, and Orville would fly for the Army near Washington, D.C.

Wilbur went to Le Mans, a town in western France. He assembled his Flyer in a factory owned by Léon Bollée, an automobile maker, whose wife Carlotta helped translate the technical conversations. Then he moved the airplane to the Hunaudières horse-racing track just outside the town. Crowds of curious people, journalists and rival aviators gathered, many of them expecting to watch the 'bluffeur' fail.

On 8 August 1908, Wilbur took off. The flight lasted only 1 minute and 45 seconds, but it was enough. The spectators watched him bank smoothly into turns, fly in circles and land gently and precisely where he wanted. No European airplane could do anything like it. The French machines of the time could fly mostly in straight lines, turning in wide, flat, skidding curves. Wilbur's Flyer swooped and banked like a bird. Among those watching was Louis Blériot, who would make his own name very soon.

The reaction was astonishing. Georges Besançon, editor of the French aviation magazine L'Aérophile, wrote that the flights had 'completely dissipated all doubts'. Many of the people who had sneered at the brothers now apologised publicly. Ernest Archdeacon, who had been so scornful, admitted that he had done the Wrights an injustice.

Wilbur stayed in France for months, moving to a military camp nearby, Camp d'Auvours, where he had more room. He flew longer and longer, often with passengers. On 7 October 1908, Edith Berg, the wife of one of the Wrights' business agents, became the first American woman to ride in an airplane; she tied a rope around her skirt so it would not blow about, and fashionable French women later copied the look. On 31 December 1908, Wilbur won the Michelin Cup with a flight of about 2 hours and 20 minutes. Wilbur, a quiet man in a cloth cap who preferred work to parties, had become one of the most famous people in Europe.

In early 1909 he moved on to Pau in southern France, where he set up a flying school, and then to Rome, where he trained Italian military pilots. Kings came to watch: the rulers of Great Britain, Spain and Italy all saw him fly. Back home in October 1909, during a big celebration in New York, Wilbur flew up the Hudson River past the city, watched by perhaps a million people, with a canoe strapped beneath the Flyer in case he had to land on the water.

sections.heading: Triumph and Tragedy at Fort Myer
paragraphs: Meanwhile, Orville was flying for the US Army at Fort Myer, Virginia, just across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C. The Army's tests were demanding. The airplane had to carry two people, stay up for an hour, and average at least 40 miles per hour, about 64 kilometres per hour. The basic price was 25,000 dollars, with a bonus of 2,500 dollars for every mile per hour faster than 40.

Orville began flying there in early September 1908 and quickly broke one record after another. On 9 September he flew for 62 minutes and 15 seconds, the first airplane flight in history to last more than an hour. Thousands of people came out to watch, including government officials. Many were seeing an airplane for the first time in their lives.

Then, on 17 September 1908, something went terribly wrong. Orville was flying with a passenger: Lieutenant Thomas Selfridge, the young Army officer from Bell's Aerial Experiment Association, who was one of the Army's official observers. A few minutes into the flight, one of the propellers split. The broken propeller hit a bracing wire, which pulled loose part of the rudder system, and the Flyer dived out of control into the ground. Orville was badly hurt, with a broken leg, several broken ribs and injuries to his hip. Selfridge suffered a serious head injury and died that evening. He was the first person ever to die in the crash of a powered airplane.

It was a heartbreaking moment, both for the Wright family and for the small world of early flying, where everyone knew everyone. Orville's sister, Katharine, took time off from her job as a teacher to stay by his side in the hospital for weeks. Investigators and the Wrights themselves studied exactly what had broken, and the brothers changed their designs to make them stronger. That habit, of studying every accident carefully so the same thing never happens again, became one of the most important traditions in aviation, as you will see in Part 18. Today an air base in Michigan, Selfridge Air National Guard Base, is named in his memory.

Orville recovered, though he suffered pain from his injuries for the rest of his life. In June 1909 he returned to Fort Myer with a new Flyer, and on 27 July 1909 he completed the official tests with a passenger aboard. The airplane beat the required speed, earning the brothers a bonus, and the US Army bought it for a total of 30,000 dollars. It became the Army's first airplane, Signal Corps Aeroplane Number 1. The doubters had gone quiet. Later that year the brothers formed the Wright Company to build airplanes for sale.

In less than six years, the Wrights had gone from 12 seconds over the sand at Kitty Hawk to selling airplanes to armies and training pilots across Europe. But the rest of the world was catching up fast. In France, dozens of inventors were building and flying their own machines. On a summer morning in July 1909, one of them, Louis Blériot, stood on the coast of northern France near Calais, looking out across the grey waters of the English Channel toward the white cliffs of England, wondering if his little monoplane could make it to the other side.

deepDive: Who flew first depends on what you mean by 'flying', and historians are careful with their definitions. Most aviation historians credit the Wrights with the first sustained, powered, controlled flights of a heavier-than-air machine carrying a pilot: on 17 December 1903 the Flyer took off under its own power from a level rail, flew forward without losing speed, was steered by its pilot and landed on ground as high as its starting point. Supporters of Alberto Santos-Dumont, especially in Brazil, argue for different rules. They point out that the Wrights' 1903 flights relied on a strong headwind and that their 1904 and 1905 flights used a falling-weight catapult, while the 14-bis rolled away on wheels in calm air before official judges. Critics of that view reply that the 1903 Flyer used no catapult at all, that wheels and catapults are a matter of take-off method rather than the core problem of flight, and that the 14-bis had no proper roll control until ailerons were added and flew only short straight hops, while the Wrights had flown 39 kilometres in circles in 1905. Witnessing matters too. The Wrights' 1903 flights had five local witnesses and a photograph, and the 1904 and 1905 flights were seen by neighbours, passengers on the trolley line and Amos Root, but they were never measured by an official body such as the Aéro-Club de France. That is why some European writers continued to doubt them until 1908. The Whitehead and Pearse claims face a different problem: not the definition, but the lack of trustworthy evidence from the time. The debate has an odd twist involving the Smithsonian Institution. After Curtiss modified and flew Samuel Langley's old Aerodrome in 1914, the Smithsonian for years labelled it the first machine 'capable' of piloted flight, angering Orville, who sent the 1903 Flyer to London's Science Museum in protest. The Smithsonian published a correction in 1942, and in 1948 the Flyer came home under an agreement with Orville's estate that the Smithsonian would not describe any earlier aircraft as capable of carrying a person under its own power in controlled flight. Some Whitehead supporters argue that this agreement makes the museum biased; most historians say the evidence, not the contract, decides the matter.
funFact: One of the first published eyewitness reports of an airplane flying in a circle appeared not in a newspaper but in Gleanings in Bee Culture, a magazine for beekeepers, written by its publisher Amos Root.

check.q: Who was killed in the crash at Fort Myer, Virginia, in September 1908, the first death in a powered airplane crash?
